title: Federalists, Anti-Federalists and Ratification
short: Federalists (Madison, Hamilton, Jay, writing as "Publius" in The Federalist) defended the Constitution; Anti-Federalists (such as "Brutus" and the "Federal Farmer") feared a distant, too-strong government without a bill of rights; New Hampshire's ratification in June 1788 made nine states.
trouble: Students think the Anti-Federalists opposed having any national government, or lost every point. Most wanted a stronger union with firmer limits; their push for a bill of rights succeeded in 1791.

blocks.html: The Convention said the Constitution would take effect when nine state conventions ratified it (Article VII). From the fall of 1787 the country argued about it in newspapers, pamphlets and speeches. It was the biggest public debate Americans had yet held.

Federalists backed the Constitution. Their best-known writing is The Federalist: 85 essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, all signed "Publius." Anti-Federalists opposed it as written. Writers such as "Brutus" and the "Federal Farmer" feared a distant, too-powerful government and the lack of a bill of rights. New Hampshire became the ninth state on June 21, 1788.

Both sides were arguing about the same question: how can a free people have a government strong enough to work but not strong enough to oppress them? Madison answered in Federalist No. 10 that a large republic is safer, because it holds so many groups that no one faction can easily take over. Brutus answered that a free republic cannot work over so large a country, because representatives would be too few and too far from the people.

doc.title: Two voices
doc.source: The Federalist No. 10 (Madison, November 1787); George Mason, Objections to the Constitution (1787)
paras: Madison: "Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens."

Mason: "There is no declaration of rights: and the laws of the general government being paramount to the laws and constitutions of the several states, the declarations of rights, in the separate states, are no security."

marks.note: Make the republic larger. Madison says size is a protection, not a danger.

marks.text: There is no declaration of rights
marks.note: Mason's first objection: the Constitution lists no rights the new government may not touch.
Supreme. Federal laws would outrank the state constitutions and their bills of rights.

blocks.title: The count to nine
blocks.q: Delaware ratified first (December 1787). By the end of May 1788, eight states had ratified. Which state made nine, and why did Virginia and New York still matter?
steps: New Hampshire ratified on June 21, 1788: the ninth state. The Constitution could now take effect.
Virginia (June 25, 89 to 79) and New York (July 26, 30 to 27) were large and stood between the other states.
A union without them would hardly work, so their close votes were watched everywhere.
Massachusetts had shown the way through: ratify now and recommend amendments. Virginia and New York did the same.
blocks.a: New Hampshire; Virginia and New York were too large and central to leave out, and their votes were close.

blocks.html: Anti-Federalists did not oppose having any national government, and they did not lose every point. Most wanted a stronger union than the Articles but with firmer limits. Their loudest demand, a bill of rights, won: Madison drafted it in 1789 and it was ratified in 1791. Check: who pushed for the Bill of Rights? The Constitution's critics.
